what_it_does: Resistive RAM (RRAM) is a type of memory chip where each cell stores data as electrical resistance rather than charge; it can also perform multiply-accumulate arithmetic directly inside the memory array, avoiding the costly data movement between separate memory and processor chips. Training a neural network normally requires computing gradients — the error signals that tell each weight how to change — which is expensive. NoiseZO sidesteps gradient computation entirely by exploiting a quirk of RRAM: when a cell is written, its resistance lands at a slightly random value (write noise). The system uses that built-in randomness as tiny random perturbations to the network's weights, and by running two forward passes (one with the perturbation, one without) it estimates how much each weight should change without ever computing a traditional gradient. The approach requires only simple forward arithmetic, making it well suited to the in-memory computing hardware where backward passes are hard to implement.
